name: Yara Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a formwork carpenter, so I build the wooden moulds that the concrete gets poured into. Right now we're on a six-storey block of flats on the old dairy site off Mill Road, and I'm on site by quarter to seven with a flask of coffee. Most of the day is plywood, props, nails and checking levels, then stripping the forms once the concrete's cured. I like the moment the pour goes in and the shape holds, but my knees and my right shoulder complain every single morning now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work with, and how long have you been doing this?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thirty-four years, all of it with my hands, and the last eleven with Hollis Concrete. I eat lunch most days with Bogdan, he's a steel fixer, and we sit on the same upturned buckets by the hoist. I've been in the carpenters' union since my second year, and I still go to branch meetings when my partner Tomas doesn't need the car. I don't use any of the AI stuff, my daughter Lena put an app on my phone and I've never opened it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype, you say. That sounds about right to me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, at the lunch buckets at least. Every few years someone comes on site with a tablet and a new system, and six months later we're back to tape measures and pencils. I'd probably share some cartoon about it in the union group chat, that's about my limit online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I get to finish my working life the way I started it. I'd still worry about my body more than any computer. Whether I can do another seven or eight years of carrying sheets of ply is the real question, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep going at Hollis, keep putting a bit into the savings, we've got about four months of bills put by. Maybe I'd finally see the physio about the shoulder instead of putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. Like getting home and finding the boiler's still working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office brings in new systems. Has any of that changed how you work so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Last year they made us log our hours on a phone app instead of the paper sheet, and half the crew still hands Bogdan's nephew their phones to do it. The ply is still heavy, the concrete is still wet, and the wind still blows the forms about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what would make the next eight years good for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lighter work for the older ones, to be honest. Let me do the setting out and checking instead of carrying props up four flights. That's a fight for the union, not for a robot.

S0.say: I told you so, it was hype all along. Every few years someone turns up on site with a tablet and a new system, and six months later we're back to tape measures and pencils.
S0.think: It means I get to finish my working life the way I started it. The real question is whether my knees and shoulder last another seven or eight years, not any computer.
S0.do: Keeps working at Hollis Concrete and keeps adding to about four months of savings. Finally books the physio for her shoulder instead of putting it off.
S0.feel: Relieved, like coming home to find the boiler still works.
S0.quote: The ply is still heavy, the concrete is still wet, and the wind still blows the forms about.
S0.fieldNote: Her biggest threat in a flat world is her own body, not technology. She frames better conditions for older workers as a union fight. Dry humour, very rooted in the physical detail of formwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many tasks in many jobs. I can picture the office getting that, less so the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the bosses' dream and the workers' bill, same as always. At the branch meeting I'd want us asking who keeps the savings when a job gets faster. I'd say it out loud, I'm not shy about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it hits the office first and reaches me late, maybe after I'm gone. But I'd feel it in small ways, more checking, more apps, a manager watching a screen instead of walking the floors. I don't want to spend my last years being told by a tablet that I'm slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a written agreement on any new kit before it comes on site. I'd keep working and keep saving, maybe twenty or thirty more a week. I would not go on a course to learn the new stuff, I'd let the younger ones do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a noise in the van you can't place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let the younger ones learn it. What if Hollis said you had to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do the minimum and grumble about it. I learned the hours app because they made me, and I'll learn the next one the same way. But I won't go home and play with it, my evenings are for Tomas and the garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The site office girls, Rosa and Deepa, who do the orders and the paperwork. That's the kind of job this eats. And maybe the labourers, if they bring in machines that carry things up the floors.

S1.say: It's the bosses' dream and the workers' bill, same as always. When a job gets faster, we need to ask who keeps the savings, and I'll say that at the branch meeting.
S1.think: I think it hits the office first and reaches me late, maybe after I'm gone. What I dread is spending my last years being watched and judged by a screen.
S1.do: Presses the union for a written agreement on any new equipment before it reaches site. Keeps working and saves an extra twenty or thirty a week, but refuses to take courses on the new tools.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like an unexplained noise in the van.
S1.quote: I don't want to spend my last years being told by a tablet that I'm slow.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry isn't losing the job but losing dignity in it, being monitored. She'll comply with new tools only under orders. Her concern goes quickly to the office staff and labourers rather than herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Robots doing the hands-on work too. That's not a picture, that's a punch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we have unions, and we'd better start shouting now. I'd be at every branch meeting and probably at a protest outside the council or wherever they'd let us stand. Online I'd share whatever the union put out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be sixty in 2028, and my pension doesn't start till sixty-six. Four months of savings doesn't stretch across six years. If robots can do formwork by then, Hollis won't keep a sixty-year-old with a bad shoulder on out of kindness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop the extras, no holiday in the caravan next summer, cancel the sports channel, and put everything into savings. I'd go to the union about early retirement deals and redundancy terms while there's still something to bargain with. And Tomas and I would have the conversation about whether his bus garage job could carry us, because I'm not going to retrain at fifty-nine to sit behind a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in the stomach, if I'm honest. Like standing on a form you haven't checked and feeling it give.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years of warning, what would you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit at the kitchen table with Tomas and every bank letter we've got and add it all up. Then I'd ring the branch secretary, Marguerite, and ask what's being done. I don't know what she'd say. I don't think anyone would have an answer that fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't retrain. Even if that was the only way to keep earning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how that sounds. But I'm fifty-eight and I left school for an apprenticeship because I'm no good at sitting still with a book. If the choice was a course or unemployment benefit, I'd probably try the course, but I'd hate every minute and I doubt the job at the end would be there.

S2.say: This is exactly why we have unions, and we'd better start shouting now. I'd be at every branch meeting and any protest they'd let us hold.
S2.think: I'd be sixty in 2028 with no pension until sixty-six and four months of savings. If a robot can do formwork, Hollis won't keep me on out of kindness.
S2.do: Cuts the caravan holiday and the sports channel and saves everything. Goes to the union about early retirement and redundancy terms, and works out with Tomas whether his bus garage wage could carry them.
S2.feel: Sick in the stomach, like feeling an unchecked form give under her feet.
S2.quote: Four months of savings doesn't stretch across six years.
S2.fieldNote: The sums are what scare her: the gap between sixty and sixty-six. She leans on the union and her partner rather than any personal reinvention. She admitted, reluctantly, that she'd try a course if forced, which softens her earlier refusal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. So 2031. I'd be sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before, but louder and for longer. I'd say we've got time to win something here, a proper bridge to pension age for older trades, and I'd say it at every meeting. I'd probably write to my MP, which I've done exactly once before, about asbestos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, sixty-three is close enough to see the end. If I can get to sixty-three and the union gets some early retirement deal, I can maybe limp across. It's still not what I planned, but it's not the cliff edge the two-year one is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, maybe an extra hundred a month, and we'd pay off the car early. I'd get the union to push for a deal for over-sixties before the robots arrive. And I'd keep turning up at Hollis every day, because the only way I get to sixty-three is by not losing this job first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. It's a long ladder instead of a fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years, compared with the last one, actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to pile up maybe another year of savings, and time for the union to fight. In two years you're just reacting. In five you can at least organise, get people to sign things, get a deal on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything different to your kids in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To Kai, yes. He's thirty and drives a forklift at a warehouse, and I'd tell him to get out of that now and into something with people, nursing like his sister maybe. I'd worry about him more than me in this one.

S3.say: We've got time to win something here: a proper bridge to pension age for older trades. I'd say it at every meeting and write to my MP for only the second time in my life.
S3.think: At sixty-three I can see the end, and with an early retirement deal I might limp across. It's not what I planned, but it's not the cliff edge of the two-year one.
S3.do: Saves about an extra hundred a month and pays off the car early. Pushes the union for an over-sixties deal and keeps turning up at Hollis so she doesn't lose the job first.
S3.feel: Anxious but able to breathe, a long ladder rather than a fall.
S3.quote: In two years you're just reacting. In five you can at least organise, get people to sign things, get a deal on paper.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns her from reacting to organising, which is where she feels strongest. Her worry shifts noticeably to her son in a warehouse job. She'd use politics, unusually for her, but only through her MP.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036. I'd be sixty-eight, so I'd be out by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still say it out loud, because it's not about me. Somebody has to make sure the young ones coming up get a fair deal, a shorter week or a share of what the machines make. I'd say it at the branch and I'd vote for whoever promised that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd probably be fine. I'd retire at sixty-six like I planned, maybe sixty-five if the knees go. The robots would arrive after I've handed in my boots, so it's my kids' problem, and their kids'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change much for myself, I'd keep working at Hollis and saving like normal. I'd stay in the union and keep going to meetings, and maybe help with the young members' training. And I'd vote on it, every chance I got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for the others, calm for myself. Is that selfish? Probably a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's your kids' problem. What would you actually say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena she's probably all right, nobody wants a robot holding their hand in hospital. Kai I'd sit down with properly. I'd tell him he's got ten years and he should use them, which is funny coming from me, who wouldn't open an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that you'd find hopeful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the union and the government got it right, maybe nobody would have to wreck their knees for thirty-four years. That would be something. I just don't trust the people at the top to share it unless they're made to.

S4.say: It's not about me, it's about the young ones coming up. They need a fair deal, a shorter week or a share of what the machines make, and I'll vote for whoever promises that.
S4.think: I'd probably be fine, retired at sixty-six or sixty-five before the robots reach formwork. Honestly, it's my kids' problem, and their kids'.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving as normal at Hollis. Stays active in the union, perhaps helping train young members, and votes on the issue at every chance.
S4.feel: Calm for herself and a bit uneasy for others, which she admits feels slightly selfish.
S4.quote: Maybe nobody would have to wreck their knees for thirty-four years. That would be something.
S4.fieldNote: Distance in time makes her calm about herself but not about others, and she named that herself. She sees a possible upside, but only if workers force the gains to be shared. She noticed the irony of telling her son to adapt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. It lands right in the gap between sixty and sixty-six, where I've got four months of savings and a body that's not going to get hired anywhere new. What would help is a proper bridge: a pension that starts early for people in heavy trades if their work disappears, and a union strong enough to make the bosses pay into it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the body. Everyone talks about robots taking the jobs, but nobody asks what thirty-four years of carrying ply does to a person. If a machine took the heavy lifting and left me the setting out, I wouldn't complain. It's who owns the machine that matters.

headlineQuote: If a machine took the heavy lifting and left me the setting out, I wouldn't complain. It's who owns the machine that matters.
portrait: Yara Wagner is a 58-year-old formwork carpenter with Hollis Concrete, a union member for over three decades who has never opened an AI app. She is calm when AI stays hype and uneasy about being monitored if change is steady. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because it falls into the six-year gap before her pension, with only four months of savings. With five or ten years she shifts to organising and worries more about her son in a warehouse. She doesn't fear machines as such, only who owns them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it lands between sixty and sixty-six, when she has four months of savings and a body no new employer would hire.
whatWouldHelp: An early pension bridge for people in heavy trades whose work disappears, and a union strong enough to make employers pay into it.
